October 19, 2026

Via Federal e-rulemaking portal



Debbie-Anne A. Reese
Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street NE, Room 1A
Washington, DC, 20426


RE: DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC; Notice of Preliminary Permit Application Accepted
for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions To Intervene, and Competing Applications (91 FR
54868)

Dear Ms. Reese,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the preliminary permit application for the DeepGreen
Western Passage Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project No. 15424-000.

Oceana is concerned about the thermal effects on the surrounding waters; marine mammal harms via
increased vessel traffic, disturbance to food sources, and acoustic impacts; fishery disruptions; and
negative impacts on Maine's coastal economy. Due to these risks, the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission (FERC) must reject DeepGreen Western Passage's Project No. 15424-000.



   I. UNDERWATER DATA CENTERS MAY DIRECTLY HARM MARINE MAMMALS
      AND FISHERIES

Because this novel industry has yet to be implemented at scale and studied, there is limited information
available on direct impacts of constructing underwater data centers. However, an understanding of the
impacts of ocean industrialization is sufficient to predict likely adverse consequences for marine
ecosystems and coastal communities.
 2



    A. Impacts to North Atlantic right whales and other marine mammals

The proposed activities could increase risks to North Atlantic right whales and other species in the
region. North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) are a critically endangered species with only
an estimated 384 whales remaining.1 In addition to right whales, other endangered marine mammals in
the area include fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus), blue whales (B. musculus), sei whales (B.
borealis), and sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus).

Food abundance

Much of the federal waters offshore Eastport, Maine are designated as North Atlantic right whale critical
habitat in the Northeast U.S. Foraging Area Unit 1 under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) due to high
concentrations of food.2 Critical habitat in the U.S. is defined as “specific areas within the geographical
area occupied by the species at the time of listing that contain physical or biological features essential to
conservation of the species and that may require special management considerations or protection”.3
Areas of the Bay of Fundy, just beyond where this project is proposed, are also identified as critical
habitat for North Atlantic right whales by Canada’s Species at Risk Act (SARA).4 Canadian critical
habitat as defined under section 2 of SARA is the “habitat necessary for the survival or recovery of a
listed wildlife species”.5 Right whales come to this area due to the dense concentrations of food. In some
years, up to two thirds of the known population have been sighted in this region, including mothers with
young calves returning from their southern nursey areas.6

Water temperature strongly controls the metabolism, development, survival and geographic distribution
of North Atlantic right whale's preferred food source, Calanus finmarchicus.7 Depending on the size and
discharge rate of the proposed underwater data centers, the water temperature may rise enough to disrupt

and body size8, any project that causes increased food stress should be prohibited.

Vessel strikes

Collisions with boats is a leading cause of North Atlantic right whale injury and death.9 They are slow,
swimming around 6 miles per hour, usually near the water’s surface.10 They are also dark in color and
lack a dorsal fin, making them very difficult to spot. Since 2017 across the U.S. and Canada, vessel
strikes have been the cause of at least 15 deaths and 14 additional injuries.11 The increase in vessel
traffic needed to scope, build, and maintain these underwater projects could lead to additional risk for
these whales.

Increased underwater noise

Ocean noise pollution is of special concern for whales and other cetaceans, as they are highly dependent
on sound as their principal sense and largely utilize acoustic cues for navigation, communication,
foraging, and predator avoidance.12

On land, data centers generate significant noise pollution, with internal noise levels reaching up to 96 A-
weighted decibels (dBA), above the 85 dBA threshold considered harmful to human hearing.13 Noise
emitting from the outside of data centers varies depending on size and but is estimated between 40 to 70

     B. Fishery impacts

Endangered Atlantic Salmon population overlap

This project also overlaps with important habitat for the endangered Gulf of Maine distinct population
segment (DPS) of Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar).16 Atlantic salmon are anadromous fish, meaning that
they spawn in fresh water, migrate to the ocean to forage and mature, and return to fresh water to spawn
and begin the cycle again.17 Unlike Pacific salmon, Atlantic salmon are iteroparous, meaning that they
can survive spawning multiple rounds and may make a repeat journey throughout their lifetimes.18
Atlantic salmon sensitive to thermal stress - negatively impacting health and in extreme conditions even
leading to mass mortality events.19

The thermal output of underwater data centers in this area has the potential to disrupt these important
migratory patterns, impacting spawning patterns and generations of salmon to come.

"Forever chemicals"

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as "forever chemicals", are found in various
parts of data centers including cooling systems, semiconductors, and hardware, due to their durability
and heat resistance.20 When constructing data centers underwater, it is likely that these chemicals will
be released into the surrounding water. Certain PFAS compounds have high bioaccumulation rates in
fish, meaning that they can be stored in the tissues of fish and may have an increased concentration in
predatory fish at higher trophic levels.21 This could translate to a higher level of PFAS in fish that
recreational and commercial anglers catch in the surrounding waters.

     II. UNDERWATER DATA CENTERS MAY NEGATIVELY IMPACT MAINE’S COASTAL
         ECONOMY

Tourism and recreation are consistently the largest employment sector in coastal economies across the
country, providing over two million American jobs and bringing in nearly $140 billion in gross domestic
product (GDP) through activities like watersports, paddling, fishing, and beachgoing that rely on healthy
marine species and habitats.22

Maine's coastal economy and cultural heritage are directly tied to the oceans. In addition to tourism and
recreation, the oceans are economically important for commercial and recreational fishing, ship and boat
building, marine transportation, and more. In Maine alone, the coastal economy provides over 57,000
jobs and yields $5.9 billion in GDP annually.23 Maine’s working waterfront supports a world class
seafood industry that was valued at over $600 million in 2025, surpassing $500 million for the 14th

consecutive year.24 Essential fish habitat is already under threat from development and pollution.
Eelgrass beds, for example, have declined by over 50% in some areas of Maine.25 These beds harbor
young shellfish and finfish, protect against storms, and boost water quality but are sensitive to growing
human impact.26

By introducing industrial infrastructure into Maine's coastal waters, underwater data centers could
threaten the state’s economic engine if there is impact on navigable waters, fisheries, or perceived
disruption to the pristine environment that underpins the state's ocean economy.

                                            CONCLUSION

The absence of studies on underwater data centers should not be mistaken for an absence of risk. We
urge FERC to reject the preliminary permit to build the DeepGreen Western Passage Subsea-Compute &
Infrastructure Hub.


Sincerely,



Julia Singer

Defense Campaign Manager
